name: Reggaeton dembow
rationale: The dembow is the backbone of reggaeton and much of today's Latin pop: a kick on every beat against a snare on the 'a' of 1 and the 'and' of 2 (boom, ch-boom, chick). Latin's 90-104 BPM is exactly reggaeton tempo. Four takes: plain with 8th hats, shaker instead of hats with a clap on the snare, an open-hat lift with a tom fill at the end of the second bar, and a half-time kick 'perreo' feel. The current latin generator has no dembow at all.

name: Tresillo pop groove
rationale: The tresillo (3+3+2: hits on beat 1, the 'and' of 2, and beat 4) is the rhythm under countless Latin-flavoured pop hits. Here the kick plays the tresillo with a straight backbeat snare, 8th hats and a 16th shaker, which gives the lighter, radio-friendly Latin pop feel the dembow doesn't cover. Bar 2 adds a push into the next bar. It also suits bright pop at the slower end of its range.

name: Discofox
rationale: Schlager is danced as Discofox: a steady four-on-the-floor kick, a clap and snare on 2 and 4, and open hi-hats on every off-beat that give it the bounce. Schlager currently borrows the EDM generator, which is too clubby and lacks the off-beat open hat. Four takes: classic, a busier one with 16th closed hats and a shaker, a lighter verse version, and one with a snare-and-tom run into the next bar for section ends. 120-129 BPM is Discofox tempo.

name: Boom bap
rationale: Classic 90s hip-hop drums for the slower end of urban (85-95 BPM): a hard snare on 2 and 4, a kick that answers it with syncopated doubles, 8th hats, and quiet ghost notes on the second snare before the backbeat. The urban generator covers the modern sparse sound; this fills the sample-based, head-nodding side. Three takes, the last with an open hat at the end of each bar.

name: Trap hats (generator)
rationale: A generator rather than fixed patterns, because what makes trap drums sound played is the hi-hat: 16ths (or 8ths in quieter sections) broken up by 32nd-note rolls placed off the downbeat, plus the odd open hat. Each song and section rolls its own placement, with a backbeat snare (usually doubled by a clap) and a sparse syncopated kick. At urban's 60-100 BPM this sits at full time, like a 140 BPM trap beat felt in half time.
